To terminate something means to bring it to a definitive, complete end. Not a pause. Not a slowdown. A full stop.

Think of it this way: when something terminates, it is over. It no longer exists, continues, or operates. The action has been concluded — either by someone's decision or by reaching a natural boundary.
What Makes It Different from "Stop" or "End"

This is important. "Stop," "end," and "terminate" can all refer to something coming to a close, but they are not identical in feel or use.

"Stop" is casual and everyday. "I stopped walking." "End" is neutral and widely used. "The movie ended." But terminate is formal, deliberate, and often carries a sense of authority or official action. It suggests that someone — or something — with power made a clear, decisive cut. It has a clinical, precise quality. You wouldn't say "I terminated my sandwich." That sounds absurd, because "terminate" is reserved for things of some weight or significance — contracts, jobs, programs, routes, pregnancies, relationships, processes.

So the word carries weight. It signals that something meaningful has been formally, officially, and completely brought to an end.

Terminates something (active, transitive): Here, a person or entity is the one doing the terminating. They are actively ending something.

  • The bank terminated his loan agreement.
  • The manager terminated the meeting abruptly.
  • The software automatically terminates idle sessions.

Something terminates (intransitive): Here, no external force is necessarily implied — the thing itself simply reaches its endpoint, its natural conclusion.

  • This road terminates at the coastline.
  • The bus service terminates at Central Station.
  • The contract terminates on December 31st.

In the intransitive use, "terminate" simply means "this is where it ends." It reaches a boundary and goes no further.
All the Major Contexts You'll Encounter

Employment: This is one of the most common uses. When a company "terminates" an employee, it means the person has been officially let go from their job — fired, dismissed. It's a formal, HR-style word. "Her employment was terminated effective immediately." It sounds cold and businesslike, which is exactly the register it's used in.

Contracts and legal agreements: A contract can be terminated, meaning the legal agreement is officially ended and neither party is obligated to fulfil its terms any longer. This can happen at the agreed-upon expiry date, or it can happen early if one party breaks the terms or both parties agree to cancel it. "Either party may terminate this agreement with 30 days' written notice."

Pregnancy: A pregnancy can be medically terminated, meaning it is deliberately ended before natural completion. This is the standard clinical and medical term used in healthcare contexts.

Transport routes: When a bus, train, or other transit route "terminates" at a location, that location is the final stop — the end of the line. The vehicle goes no further. "This train terminates at Paddington." This is a very standard announcement you hear in transit systems.

Computing and technology: A program, process, or application can be terminated — meaning it is shut down or forcibly stopped. "The system terminated the unresponsive process." If you've ever seen an error message saying a program has "been terminated," it means the application was stopped, either by the system or the user.

Conversations, negotiations, or relationships: Though less common, you can terminate a conversation or a relationship. "He terminated the call without warning." This usage emphasises the abruptness, finality, and deliberateness of the ending — it wasn't a natural fading away; someone actively cut it off.

Military and intelligence (euphemism): In spy fiction and real-world intelligence contexts, "terminate" is used as a cold euphemism for killing someone. "The order was to terminate the target." This usage is well-known enough to understand when you encounter it, especially in films, novels, or news.

You'll often see "terminate" used in the passive voice, especially in formal and professional writing, because it softens the directness of who made the decision:

  • Active: "The company terminated his contract." (Clear — the company did it.)
  • Passive: "His contract was terminated." (Vaguer — we're not specifying who terminated it.)

The passive form is extremely common in corporate and legal language, precisely because it sounds more neutral and detached.

Always remember: terminate is a formal word. It belongs to professional, legal, medical, technical, and official contexts. It is not conversational. Nobody says "I terminated my gym session early." They'd say "I cut my gym session short" or "I left early."

When you see or hear "terminate," it signals that something official is happening — a deliberate, authoritative ending has taken place or is being referred to. The word has a slightly cold, impersonal quality, which is why it's favoured in corporate and legal settings where emotions are kept out of the language.

To terminate means to formally, deliberately, and completely bring something to an end — whether that's a job, a contract, a process, a route, or any other thing of significance — with a tone of authority, finality, and precision.
